outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your poem, refined for eloquence while preserving its original imagery, structure, and meaning:

---

In Tunis we attempt to speak of divorce
And dying, but surrender instead to lounging
With rug merchants beneath a plum tree.
From its corner, the lamb's severed head
Watches flies drink from its eyes
As its fat dissolves into the fire.
Light rinses the edge of your sandal,
The two wasps that adorn the haze
Of the screened window. My grandmother
Would have cherished a night like this.
In the wind chimes I hear her tea cart,
Its china rattling across Cook Street's
Stony yard, one summer when I was always
Thirsty, and she moved like a figure
On a clock—from my lawn chair to the cart,
Or swabbing me with alcohol, or cutting
My hair with a straight razor.
I was a week out of the hospital then.
Beneath my breasts, an incision lay crossed
With stitches of surgical thread.
The scalpel came so close it brushed
My heart with a fleeting kiss. I nearly died.
Years later, I can still see the skin
Flutter along the inside of my left breast,
And my heart limps like a great-uncle
Who, being both Jew and lame,
Was dragged by Cossacks across the steppes—
Until he became a friend, begging a favor
Of a horse that ran so hard, so flawlessly
Hard, that the green grass rose to meet him.

---

I preserved the poem's narrative arc, emotional weight, and vivid imagery while smoothing transitions, tightening word choices (e.g., "attempt" for "try," "dissolves" for "disappear," "flawlessly" for "perfectly"), and enhancing rhythmic flow. Let me know if you'd like a version with different emphasis—more spare and stark, or more lyrical and ornate.

In the Tunisian marketplace, conversations about separation
And mortality dissolve into idle afternoons, reclining
With carpet sellers beneath fruit-laden branches.
From where it rests, the lamb's decapitated head
Observes insects sipping moisture from its sockets
As its grease dissolves into the flames below.
Sunlight washes across your sandal's edge,
Where paired wasps decorate the hazy
Mesh of the window screen. My grandmother
Would have cherished an evening such as this one.
Within the wind chimes' music, her tea trolley echoes,
Its porcelain clattering across Cook Street's
Gravel courtyard during that summer of endless
Thirst, when she traveled like clockwork
Between my chair and her cart,
Dabbing me with antiseptic, or trimming
My hair using an old-fashioned blade.
Seven days had passed since my hospital release.
Below my chest, a surgical cut remained
Closed with medical thread and stitching.
The blade's precision brought it dangerously
Near my heart, granting it a fleeting touch. Death nearly claimed me.
Even now, decades later, I perceive that tremor
Beneath the surface of my left breast,
And my heart drags itself like some distant relative—
A great-uncle who, being both Hebrew and crippled,
Was pulled across the frozen plains by Cossack riders.
He transformed into someone requesting kindness
From a horse whose gallop was so forceful, so flawlessly
Powerful, that the emerald fields lifted upward to greet him.

# Fragments of Memory

In Tunis, the conversation had turned, as such conversations do, toward the weightier matters of life—divorce, death, the slow unraveling of things once thought permanent. But somewhere between one sentence and the next, the gravity of it all seemed to lose its hold. The words dissolved into laughter and the easy rhythm of bargaining with rug merchants who sat cross-legged beneath the deep shade of a plum tree. The air was thick with the particular textures of that place: the severed head of a sacrificial lamb resting nearby, its presence both mundane and startling, and the low, insistent drone of wasps circling somewhere close, drawn by sweetness or blood or both. It was easier, in that moment, to let the heaviness go—to trade philosophy for the simple pleasure of haggling over the price of wool and dye, to let the senses crowd out the mind's darker corridors.

And then, without warning, the grandmother arrives—summoned not by will but by sound. It is the wind chimes that do it, their delicate clatter catching some thread in memory and pulling it taut. Suddenly she is there again, and with her, an entire summer unfolds: the particular groan and rattle of her tea cart as it rolled across a stony yard, wheels catching on uneven ground, the sound as distinct as a voice. She is bending down, offering water to a child parched from the heat, her hands moving with the unhurried tenderness of someone who has spent a lifetime tending to small needs. The memory is not dramatic—it is only a woman and a thirsty child and the sun overhead—but it carries the weight of everything unspoken between generations, the love that expresses itself not in words but in gestures repeated until they become ritual.

The body, too, holds its own memories. A week after leaving the hospital following a serious surgery, the speaker becomes intimately acquainted with the strange topography of recovery: the incision tracing its careful line beneath the breasts, still raw, still new. There is something disquieting in knowing how close the scalpel came to the heart—not metaphorically, but literally, the blade moving through flesh mere inches from the organ that keeps everything running. This proximity lingers long after the wound itself has closed, a kind of knowledge the body doesn't forget even when the mind moves on.

Years pass, and still the heart carries some residue of that closeness, some subtle alteration in its rhythm or gait. The speaker describes it now as moving the way their great-uncle once moved—lame, uneven, marked by old injury. He was a Jewish man who had survived the brutality of cossacks, his body forever changed by violence that history books might summarize in a single sentence but that lived in him as a daily, physical fact. The heart's imperfect beat becomes an inheritance, a way of carrying his suffering forward in the body's own private language.

But even trauma, held long enough in memory, begins to shift and transform. The great-uncle's story—the horse, the dragging, the violence of it—becomes something else entirely when viewed through the strange alchemy of time and imagination. The horse that dragged him ran with such ferocious, unstoppable power that the very grass beneath seemed to rise up to meet him, as though the earth itself were reaching out in welcome rather than injury. Suffering and transcendence blur together in this image, the horror of the original moment giving way to something almost sacred—a vision in which pain becomes a kind of flight, and the body being dragged across the ground becomes, paradoxically, a body being lifted, met, embraced by the very world that wounded it.
outputs.L4:
**Tunis, Revisited**

The medina wakes before the heat does,
copper pots clanging like distant church bells,
and already the butcher has hung his wares—
a lamb's head, eyes clouded to milk,
tongue lolling gray-pink over the counter's edge,
flies stitching their small black seams around it.
I stand in the press of bodies,
the vendors calling out in Arabic and French,
their voices braided with the smell of cumin,
orange rind, diesel, and something underneath—
blood, sweet and mineral, soaking into sawdust.

I am thirty-four years old in this market
and also six, in a hospital bed in another country,
my chest cracked open like a pomegranate
to let the surgeons reach the small mistake
lodged near my heart. I remember the smell
of iodine instead of cumin, the particular silence
of machines instead of vendors' cries,
my grandmother's hand—the only warm thing
in that cold fluorescent room—
her rings pressing crescents into my palm
as if she could carve her own survival into mine.

She never spoke of Odessa, not directly,
only in fragments dropped like crumbs
I had to gather myself: a chicken coop,
a winter with no bread, a brother
who could not run because of his leg,
twisted since birth, dragging behind him
like an afterthought God forgot to finish.

I did not know his name until I was grown.
Usher. My great-uncle, lame,
who they said outran the cossacks anyway—
not on his own legs, but slung
across the back of a neighbor's horse,
his bad foot flopping against the animal's flank
like a metronome keeping the rhythm
of some terrible, ongoing music.
The hooves struck sparks from frozen ground.
Behind him, smoke. Before him, more smoke.
He held on the way you hold on
to something you don't yet know
you'll need to pass down—
this lesson in the body's stubborn arithmetic,
how it insists on continuing
past every reasonable stopping point.

Here in Tunis, the lamb's head stares past me
at something I cannot see,
and I think of my own scar,
pale seam beneath my shirt,
and my grandmother's hands,
and Usher's foot beating time
against a horse's heaving side,
and how none of us chose
to be the ones who lived,
only found ourselves, afterward,
still breathing, still standing
in some market or another,
the future unspooling before us
like a bolt of cloth,
uncut, unmeasured,
waiting to be made into something.
outputs.L5:
# Tunis: A City Where Past Meets Present

Tunis, the vibrant capital of Tunisia, stands as a remarkable blend of ancient traditions and modern life. Nestled along the Mediterranean coast, this North African city has captivated visitors for centuries with its rich history and cultural diversity.

At the heart of Tunis lies the Medina, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating back to the 7th century. Walking through its narrow, winding streets, visitors encounter a labyrinth of souks filled with spices, textiles, and traditional crafts. The Medina is home to numerous mosques, palaces, and madrasas, each telling a story of the city's Islamic golden age.

Tunis carries within it echoes of ancient Carthage, the legendary civilization that once rivaled Rome for Mediterranean dominance. Just a short distance from the modern city center, the ruins of Carthage offer a glimpse into this powerful ancient empire, with its impressive baths, villas, and archaeological treasures scattered across the landscape.

The city's identity has been shaped by centuries of diverse influences, including Berber, Arab, Ottoman, and French colonial heritage. This multicultural history is reflected in the architecture, cuisine, and daily life of Tunis today. The elegant French colonial buildings along Avenue Habib Bourguiba stand in contrast with the ancient Arab-Islamic structures of the old city, creating a fascinating urban tapestry.

Modern Tunis functions as the political, economic, and cultural center of Tunisia. The city buzzes with activity, from bustling cafes where locals gather to discuss politics and daily life, to vibrant markets offering fresh produce and local delicacies. Tunisian cuisine, with its distinctive use of harissa, olive oil, and fresh seafood, reflects the city's Mediterranean location and cultural fusion.

Beyond its historical sites, Tunis serves as a gateway to explore the broader wonders of Tunisia, including the stunning coastal towns of Sidi Bou Said, with its iconic blue and white architecture, and the golden beaches that stretch along the coastline.

Tunis continues to evolve as a dynamic urban center, balancing preservation of its remarkable heritage with the demands of contemporary life. The city remains a testament to human resilience and cultural richness, inviting travelers to discover the layers of history embedded within its streets, monuments, and vibrant communities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem that moves between a scene in Tunis and a childhood memory of a grandmother, weaving in imagery of an open-air market and a lamb roasting on a fire.
counterfactuals.output:
**Medina Light**

The alley in Tunis breathes cumin and diesel smoke,
brass trays balanced on the heads of boys
who don't look where they're going
because they already know.

I am here and I am seven,
standing in my grandmother's kitchen
in a city she never saw,
watching her hands disappear into flour
like they were returning something borrowed.

The souk unfolds its cloth of color—
saffron mountains, olives swimming black in brine,
a woman calling out the price of mint
as if it were a secret she was tired of keeping.
Somewhere behind the stalls,
a lamb turns slowly on its spit,
fat hissing into coals,
the smoke curling upward like a prayer
nobody translated correctly.

My grandmother's hands smelled like that smoke.
Not lamb exactly—
something older, something that came before the meat,
the smell of fire itself,
of her leaning over a stove
in a kitchen three thousand miles from here,
singing to a pot in a language
I only half remember now.

In Tunis, the vendor turns the spit again.
The fire snaps. A child laughs somewhere unseen.
I think of her apron, flour-dusted,
the way she'd pull bread from the oven
like she was lifting something out of the sea.

The market moves around me—
copper pots, embroidered slippers,
a boy selling roses for a dinar each,
and underneath it all, the low gold light
of coals keeping their secret,
turning meat to memory,
memory to smoke,
smoke to whatever this is—
this standing between two places,
this tasting of thyme and rosemary
on a wind that carries her voice
from a kitchen that no longer exists
into a market that never knew her name.

The lamb turns.
The bread cools on my grandmother's counter,
decades away.
Both fires burning
in the same small, aching hour.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyric poem about surviving heart surgery as a child, blending sensory details of recovery with a surreal family memory involving Cossacks and a horse.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Scar Remembers

They tell me I was six, my chest
cracked open like a pomegranate,
the surgeon's hands moving through the red
architecture of my small, unfinished heart.
I don't remember pain—only the after:
gauze and fluorescent hum, the taste
of orange popsicle bleeding sugar
onto a tongue too tired to swallow,
my mother's face folding and unfolding
above me like a paper lantern.

The morphine gave me horses.

Not real ones—memory-horses,
borrowed from my grandmother's stories,
the ones she told in her cracked Ukrainian,
rocking in the kitchen chair
while snow ticked against the window
like something trying to get in.
She said the Cossacks came at dusk,
their coats the color of wet bark,
riding low and fast across the wheat,
and her own mother pressed her down
into the cellar's dark mouth of jars—
pickled beets, the sweat-smell of onions—
told her: *don't breathe, don't breathe,
be small as a seed, be nothing at all.*

In the hospital bed, half-dreaming,
I became that girl becoming smaller,
my sternum wired shut like a gate
between two countries—the one
where the heart simply beats, unremarked,
and the one where it must be watched,
counted, coaxed, a nervous bird
kept in a cage of new bone.

I heard hooves in the hallway carts,
in the nurses' rubber-soled retreat,
in my own pulse pressing its small fist
against the bandage, insistent,
proving itself alive, alive—
each beat a horse crossing a field
that no one, this time, would burn.

Now the scar is old rope, pale
as a river seen from far above.
I trace it sometimes in the dark
and feel the wheat give way beneath
some ancestral, thundering weight,
feel my grandmother's held breath
still moving through me, feel the doctors'
careful hands, the popsicle sweetness,
the machines that sang all night
their steady, arrhythmic lullabies—

and understand: survival is a stitching
of separate wounds into one thread,
the body remembering every crossing,
every hoofbeat, every quiet cellar,
every small mouth learning how to say
*I lived, I lived, I lived.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Mark Doty or Larry Levis that mixes travel imagery from North Africa with intimate family history and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tangier, Afterward**

I keep thinking of my father's hands, how they shook
lifting the glass of mint tea in that café off the Grand Socco,
the sugar cubes piled like something devotional,
and how the boy who brought it wore his grief so lightly,
balancing the tray above the crowd's bright noise
as if sorrow were only another thing you carried,
weightless once you learned the trick of it.

This was the year my father's heart had started
its long negotiation with silence,
and I flew him to the place he'd always wanted—
the blue doors of Chefchaouen, the medina's narrow lung
opening and closing around us like something breathing
badly, beautifully, the muezzin's call at dusk
unspooling over rooftops the color of unripe apricots.

I remember he could not climb the last hill to the kasbah,
sat instead on a low wall where an old man sold sprigs
of jasmine threaded onto reeds, and my father bought one,
held it the way he once held a cigarette he'd quit for decades,
some gesture the body keeps after the reason's gone.

Larry Levis wrote that the dead don't leave us—
they enter the grain of the wood, the pattern of a rug
some Berber woman knotted with her mother's hands
in a village whose name means nothing to us now,
though we bought that rug, dragged it home,
and it still holds, faintly, the smell of the souk:
cumin, wet wool, diesel, someone's cooking fire.

I think of my father dying two winters later
in a hospital room with a window that opened onto nothing—
a parking garage, its concrete decks like strata
in a cliff face somewhere in the Atlas Mountains
we never got to see, the guidebook still packed
in a box in my closet, its pages soft
with a humidity that was never Moroccan,
just the damp of grief, folding paper in on itself.

What I want to say is: the world doesn't end
where the body does. Or: I carried him
through those blue streets the way I carry him now,
some cellular memory of jasmine and diesel and salt,
the Atlantic slapping at the ramparts of the old city
we walked at dusk, his hand on my arm
lighter than it should have been, lighter
than any weight I thought love was supposed to bear.

The dead take up so little room, and so much.
I keep the jasmine sprig, dried now, pressed
in a book of poems he never read.
Somewhere in Tangier a boy is still carrying tea
through a crowd of strangers, the glass sweating,
the sugar dissolving into something
neither of us will ever taste again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a long-lined, image-heavy poem that begins with a couple avoiding a difficult conversation abroad, then drifts into memories of illness, grandmother's care, and ancestral trauma.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Water Carries**

We sit at a café in a city that isn't ours, the awning striped red and white like a peppermint someone forgot to unwrap, and you stir sugar into coffee you don't drink, three times, four, the spoon clinking like a small bell no one answers.

Neither of us says the thing. Instead we watch a pigeon limp across cobblestones slick with yesterday's rain, dragging one foot like a suitcase with a broken wheel, and I think how strange it is that we flew four thousand miles to sit in silence we could have brought from home for free.

The waiter refills water we haven't asked for. Somewhere a church bell counts an hour neither of us is keeping track of. You look at the horizon like it might answer for you, the sea doing that thing where it turns from blue to the color of a healing bruise, green-gray, uncertain of itself.

And this is how memory works — sideways, unbidden — because suddenly I am eleven years old again, home from school with a fever that made the wallpaper roses breathe, my grandmother's hand a cool flat stone against my forehead, testing, testing, the way you'd check bread for doneness.

She smelled of onions and Nivea cream and the particular sourness of aspirin dissolved in water she made me drink in three swallows, no more, no less, some private arithmetic of care passed down through her hands like a recipe with no measurements, just knowing.

She'd hum something in a language that wasn't quite the one we spoke at school, older, worn soft at the edges like a coin rubbed thin from pocket to pocket, and I didn't know then that the song was older than her mother too, that it had crossed a border once in someone's mouth, hidden like contraband, like a name.

I didn't know about the camp, or the forest, or the years she folded into the back drawer of herself the way you fold a letter you can't bear to read again but can't throw away — I only knew her hands, dry as paper, sure as prayer, pressing a damp cloth to my temples at 3 a.m. while my mother slept, exhausted, in the next room.

Illness in that house was never just illness. It was inheritance rehearsing itself in a child's small body — fever as a kind of echo, my grandmother's eyes going distant mid-hum, somewhere else, some other sickroom, some other child she couldn't save, some other war she carried in her sternum like a second heart that never fully healed.

Now the pigeon in this foreign square finds a crust of bread and does not share it, and you finally speak, not about us, but about the tide, how it's coming in faster than the map suggested, and I understand this is how you say I'm afraid — obliquely, through weather, the way my grandmother said I love you through broth and clean sheets and the particular folding of a fever-soaked cloth, cool side out, always.

The water rises toward our ankles though we haven't moved our chairs. Some conversations arrive the way illness does — quietly, in the body, long before the mouth finds language for it — and some things get inherited whether we ask for them or not: her hands in my hands now reaching for you, testing your forehead out of habit, out of love that skipped a war, a border, a century, and landed here, in this ordinary, terrible tenderness, still deciding what it's allowed to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective, narrative poem that uses a foreign setting (like Tunis) as a springboard into personal history—chronic illness, a near-death experience, and a Jewish ancestor's suffering under the Cossacks.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tunis, Late Light**

I.
The medina swallows me before noon,
blue doors like sutured wounds along white walls,
and somewhere a muezzin unspools his call
over rooftops stacked like vertebrae.
I buy nothing. I only walk,
letting the alley narrow until I forget
which country holds my passport,
which century holds my name.

An old man grinds cardamom by hand,
the smell rising sweet and bruised,
and it is this—not the minaret, not the sea
glimpsed blue between buildings—
that opens the trapdoor in my chest
where the hospital still waits, humming.

II.
Nineteen, the fever that would not break.
Machines translating my body into numbers
nurses whispered like a foreign tongue.
I remember the ceiling tile with the water stain
shaped like a country I could not name,
how I studied it for hours, deciding
it was the last thing I would choose to look at.
The doctors' voices came from very far away,
as if already eulogizing.

I did not see light. I did not float.
I only felt the narrowing—
the way this alley narrows now—
walls pressing close enough to read
each crack as a sentence I might finish
or might not.

I finished it. Somehow the fever broke
like weather, like a decision
made by someone other than myself.

III.
My great-grandmother crossed an ocean
carrying only what fit inside a shawl—
some coins, a spoon, the memory of hooves.
The Cossacks came in autumn, she said,
though autumn in the shtetl
meant nothing but the color of dread,
gold leaves indifferent to the screaming.
Her sister did not make it to the wagon.
Her father's beard, she said, was full of blood
he did not have time to wipe away
before the dying.

She carried this the way I carry
the ceiling tile, the water stain,
the numbers on machines—
proof that the body remembers
what the mind tries to fold small enough
to fit inside a pocket, inside a poem,
inside the space between two words
where grief lives without a passport,
stateless, permanent.

IV.
Here in Tunis the light turns copper
and the muezzin calls again,
different hour, same devotion,
and I think: we are all just bodies
that survived something,
carrying the ones who didn't
like a second skeleton.

I did not choose to live
any more than she chose to run,
any more than the fever chose to break
instead of taking me
the way it took so many others
whose names I'll never learn to say correctly.

The alley opens finally to the sea,
that old blue indifference,
and I stand at the edge of a continent
that is not mine, thinking of hooves,
of ceiling tiles, of my great-grandmother's hands
folding the last of her home into a shawl,
and how survival is not triumph—
it is only the plain fact
of still standing here,
still salt-stung, still breathing,
still someone's inheritance
walking towards the water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
